title: Why I Closed a Business I'd Spent 15 Years Building
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Summer Mulder explains the real reasoning behind closing the business she built and ran for fifteen years, rejecting the idea that exhaustion alone was the cause. She lays out a personal decision framework -- picturing the business gone during a good month rather than a bad one -- to distinguish genuine clarity from burnout-driven flight, and reflects on the leadership lesson that owning a business fully means owning both its failures and its freedom.
points: Argues exhaustion is an unreliable signal for a leader deciding whether to quit, since a bad month can make almost any decision feel like relief.
Offers a sharper test: picture walking away during a strong month, when there's no pain to escape from, and see if the relief still holds.
Describes the shift from resenting her team for 'clocking out' to realizing that carrying the business's risk alone was never their job -- it was a leadership choice she made.
Frames the real diagnostic question as identifying the one constraint that, if solved, would make the business work, then asking honestly whether solving it would still matter.
quotes: I don’t mean that you should beat yourself up. I mean that when you own it, you feel free.
Exhaustion lies to you. It tells you the business is broken when what’s actually breaking is your capacity, and if you make a permanent decision in that state, you’ll regret it.
You have to picture it gone when things are good. On a strong month, a full pipeline, a win.
For years I thought the job of my leadership was to be likeable, to keep everyone safe and content, to make sure the people around me never felt the ground move.
What’s the one constraint that, if you solved it, would make this business actually work?
